item.description:
### Added - **Federal compliance frameworks:** FedRAMP Moderate, FedRAMP High, GovRAMP Moderate, IRS Publication 1075 and Federal Zero Trust. FedRAMP, GovRAMP and IRS 1075 map as NIST 800-53 does, with the controls each baseline selects (FedRAMP High and IRS 1075 add controls such as preventing exfiltration and seeing into encrypted traffic). Federal Zero Trust maps to CISA's TIC 3.0 security capabilities and OMB memo M-22-09. FedRAMP and Federal Zero Trust add the CUI-Markings DLP rule. - **Customer Intake, compliance profile:** a POV's compliance framework is now picked once, on Customer Intake, with Internet Access or AI Guard in scope. The frameworks are grouped as on the Framework step, the hint says what the one picked covers and which one the preset suggests, and the preset picks it to start with. Filling the modules makes it Internet Access's framework (your rule choices stay) and gives AI Guard the matching profile. While a POV is open, a change of the profile reaches Internet Access and AI Guard at once, without filling the modules again (the tier and your other changes stay); the Framework step shows it without changing it, Load Selections keeps it, and AI Guard always uses the matching profile (only Monitor or Block is picked there). POVs saved before take the framework they had. With no POV open, or the product out of the POV's scope, the Framework step and AI Guard work as before. - **Federal / public sector preset:** FedRAMP Moderate as the compliance profile, case management, financial management and HR applications on Private Access, and Login.gov, USAJOBS and SAM.gov in Digital Experience; its DLP test file is the public sector one. Private Access has a matching Federal and public sector template. - **IRS Publication 1075:** a new FTI-Records DLP rule on a new custom dictionary, created in your tenant like the others, that finds Federal Tax Information labels and references to IRC section 6103 ("IRC §6103", "26 U.S.C. 6103"). It starts by monitoring, like every DLP rule. AI Guard has a matching IRS Pub 1075 compliance profile, and the POV test kit an FTI-marked memo to test it with. - **Rules, every rule maps or says why:** with a compliance framework, each rule now shows the controls it maps to (point at one for its name), or, when it maps to none, why: Zscaler best practice, differentiating use case, operational, privacy or weakens protection, with a line on what the rule does. Each policy type says how many of its rules map, a line above the rules counts the rules and the tenant-wide settings groups that map (in a POV, it says the framework was chosen on Customer Intake), and the tenant-wide settings are listed after the rules. A DLP rule's reason follows its action, as its controls do; another rule you set to another action says so in its line. With the ZTH Ebook tier, with a framework, its URL, firewall and SSL rules say they're ZTH Ebook's own policy. With CIPA, the URL & Cloud App Settings group, which turns on ZIA's CIPA Compliance rule and SafeSearch, maps to CIPA's technology protection measure. - **Review, Compliance Evidence:** the counts match the Rules page, and a "Not mapped" list gives each rule and settings group that maps to none of the framework's controls, with why. The summary report gives the reason in place of the controls. - **Compliance pack:** on Rules and on each Active POV's Prove it & test kit tab, for the chosen compliance framework: a control mapping report (CSV, or a page to print or save as PDF, with the counts and each control's description) listing every rule and each tenant-wide settings group (switched-off and left-out ones as Off) with its controls or why it has none (in a POV with Private Access, its ZPA policies too); a policy export (JSON and CSV) of the rules Apply would create, to review before Apply; and a test plan that groups the POV's tests by the controls they show, with a row for each DLP rule, the Prove it target and a blank Result column (a test of a rule whose action you changed says so). Everything is made on your Mac from your choices: nothing is read from the tenant, and no file holds who the rules apply to, the isolation profile, the certificate, the tenant captured rules came from or any secret. - **POV test kit, a file per DLP rule:** the kit now starts with a test file for each DLP rule your POV makes, named for its compliance framework and made from what that rule looks for, such as test card numbers, magnetic stripe track data on test cards (back in the kit), Medicare and medical record numbers, tax IDs, EU identifiers, CUI markings, criminal justice and student record terms, draft filings and Federal Tax Information labels. The credentials file holds only AWS's published documentation example keys. Rules for content the app doesn't make (offensive language, self-harm, source code, legal documents, resumes) say what to use instead. Each save makes new data.
### Fixed - **Build the POV:** Edit on AI Guard now opens the AI Guard page, not Security Tier, and Edit on Internet Access opens Customize. - **POV test kit:** NIST 800-53 POVs now get the CUI-marked memo too, since that framework adds the CUI-Markings rule. The memo now follows the DLP rules the wizard makes, so FedRAMP and Federal Zero Trust POVs get it as well, and Permissive POVs, which don't get that rule, no longer do. - **Policy Simulator:** a rule condition the simulator can't check now makes that rule "unknown" (listed as one that could change the result) instead of being ignored. Before, a rule whose only conditions were ones it couldn't check matched every destination: the predefined Office 365 and UCaaS One Click rules, for example, allowed everything in the firewall, and UCaaS One Click's Do Not Decrypt meant every HTTPS site was taken as not inspected. The same goes for source countries (the wizard's FW-Geo-Block-In no longer blocks every SSH, RDP and FTP connection), device trust, platforms, source IP groups, time windows in SSL Inspection and Sandbox, and File Type Control's password-protected, active content, unscannable and size conditions. - **Policy Simulator:** a File Type Control rule for uploads and downloads now matches either one. Before, it never matched, so the wizard's FTC-Block-PW-Archives didn't show at all; now a ZIP or RAR download is listed as one it could block (password protection can't be seen). - **Policy Simulator:** rules for cloud apps (such as Zoom or Webex) now match the cloud app Zscaler's lookup names for the destination, and don't match when it names none. For a wildcard destination, which is looked up as one sample host, they're unknown, since other subdomains may be other apps. When an SSL Inspection rule that might apply would change whether HTTPS is decrypted, the result says so: URL Filtering rules on the CONNECT or GET method alone, which depend on it, are shown as what could change the result instead of being ruled out, and DLP's content condition stays, "if HTTPS is decrypted". DNS Control rules on the resolved IP's category, and the rule that redirects to Private Access's resolver, now apply only to destinations they cover (a rule on IP addresses is unknown when the name's addresses aren't known). File type categories on Sandbox, File Type Control and DLP rules now count. - **Prove it:** the rules it names as ones that could decide first are no longer described as limited only to users, groups, locations or times. - **Policy Simulator, Block it:** the warning that a rule above the new one matches all traffic no longer shows for a rule limited by app service groups, cloud apps, countries or other conditions. - **Policy Simulator:** app service groups (the Office 365 and UCaaS One Click rules in Firewall, DNS Control and Cloud & Branch Connector forwarding) are now checked: a hostname against the service's published domains, and an IP address against the service's ranges from your Client Connector IP-based app definitions and, for Office 365, Microsoft's published list. Loading a tenant's policy downloads that list from Microsoft (endpoints.office.com) when a rule uses the Office 365 group; nothing about your tenant is sent, and a saved snapshot keeps it. An IP address whose service ranges aren't known is still unknown. - **Policy Simulator:** when Microsoft's Office 365 list couldn't be downloaded, an Office 365 One Click rule is now unknown for a hostname that isn't one of the Office 365 domains the simulator knows, or an IP address outside your Client Connector definitions, instead of not matching, since it may be on Microsoft's list. A wildcard host or a CIDR range that's only partly in a service's domains or ranges is unknown for its One Click rule too. The download now identifies itself only as the app, without its version, the macOS version or your languages. - **Prove it:** a Firewall or DNS check whose rules use the Office 365 app service group now downloads Microsoft's Office 365 list too, so it agrees with the Policy Simulator (a Microsoft host only on that list matches the Office 365 One Click rule in both). The list is kept in memory for an hour while you stay connected to that tenant; if the download fails, the result says so. - **Policy Simulator:** a policy set that couldn't be read when the policy was loaded (Zscaler timed out, for example) no longer looks as if no rule matched. Its module shows "Not evaluated" and takes no part in the result, and a "Couldn't fully run" note above the result (and above a comparison) names what wasn't checked and why, and says when Zscaler timed out. A category or user lookup that fails while simulating is named there too, with what it means for the result. Bulk Test has a "Not evaluated (failed/timeout)" column for the same. Cloud App Control counts too when the destination is a cloud app its rules would have checked, including when only some of its rule types couldn't be read and none of the rules read name the app. In Bulk Test such a row is "not fully evaluated": it no longer counts as meeting its expected result, it's always among the flagged rows (with why, even when only some rows have an expected result), and the counts show how many there are. - **Policy Simulator:** every simulation, Category Lookup and Bulk Test run now asks Zscaler again for the destination's categories and the user's groups (and Private Access's SCIM groups), so a result never rests on an earlier answer. Each simulation uses one of Zscaler's URL lookups. - **Policy Simulator:** while a new simulation runs, the previous result, comparison and checks from this Mac no longer stay on screen, and loading other policies clears a comparison. A simulation still running when other policies are loaded no longer shows its answer under them; one running when the policy is read again or a change is rehearsed runs again on the policy as it is now. - **Policy Simulator, Bulk Test:** users are looked up in ZIdentity too, as in a single simulation, and also when **Look up Zscaler categories** is off. A user lookup that fails is asked again for the next row with that user, instead of leaving that user without groups for the rest of the test. - **Apply:** when creating something (an AI Guard object, a ZIA DLP rule, a Client Connector forwarding profile, a Policy Simulator change) fails before it leaves your Mac (the host isn't found, the connection is refused, or the server's certificate isn't trusted), or any change fails because signing in to Zscaler failed, the app now says what went wrong instead of that it may have been made, and doesn't activate ZIA for it. A change that times out or loses its connection, and an update or delete that fails this way, still says it may have been made, since it may have gone through. - **Client Connector › Edit Existing Profiles:** a forwarding profile whose list couldn't be read before the edit was sent is no longer recorded as edited. - **Quitting while a change runs:** while a change to the tenant is running, the window can't be closed, and quitting (⌘Q, logging out or restarting, or installing an update) asks first. **Keep Running** lets it finish; **Quit Anyway** stops it partway, as quitting did before. An update you chose to install then installs the next time you quit, and the app opens again.
### Changed - **Policy Simulator:** Save Snapshot now says when the snapshot is saved. - **CSV files:** the test kit's files now quote every cell, as the licences list does, and a cell that a spreadsheet would read as a formula starts with an apostrophe. - **Compliance Evidence:** a DLP rule's controls now follow what it does with a match. While it monitors (Allow, the default) it lists the framework's monitoring and audit controls, such as HIPAA 164.312(b) and 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) or NIST 800-53 SI-4 and AU-12; set it to Block on Rules and it lists the controls for stopping data from leaving, as before. Endpoint DLP rules, which only monitor, list the monitoring controls. Review, the dry run and the summary report show the controls for the action you chose. - **Compliance Evidence:** the framework mappings were reviewed against the reference wizard's latest mapping, and the controls that fit were added: for example NIST 800-53 SC-44 on Sandbox, SC-21 on the Trusted Resolver, AC-20 on the Cloud App Control rules, and PCI 10.6, HITRUST 09.af and CIS 8.4 on the NTP rule. GDPR now cites Art.32(1)(b) instead of the whole Art.32. CJIS now maps as NIST 800-53 does, with the controls the CJIS Security Policy v6.1 selects, so far more rules show CJIS evidence. CMMC Level 1's external-connections practice (AC.L1-b.1.iii) is now cited on the Cloud App Control rules, where NIST 800-171's 3.1.20 is, and no longer on the URL Filtering blocks. - **Compliance Evidence:** Malware Protection and Advanced Threat Protection now each list the controls for what their own page does. Before, both listed the same controls, so Malware Protection (file scanning) also claimed the mobile code, phishing and intrusion prevention controls only Advanced Threat Protection meets. - **CJIS:** the CJI Records dictionary now cites the CJIS Security Policy v6.1, the version the framework names. A dictionary already in your tenant keeps its description. - **Framework step:** the frameworks are grouped by who they're for: Healthcare, Finance, Education, General, Federal and Any industry. - **Compliance Evidence:** NIST 800-53 now also cites AC-4(4), flow control of encrypted information, on the SSL inspect-all and QUIC block rules. - **AI Guard:** with FedRAMP, GovRAMP or Federal Zero Trust as the ZIA framework, the compliance profile starts on NIST 800-53. - **Selections and Active POVs:** a POV whose framework this version doesn't have now resumes with no framework and says so, as a selections file already did.
